title: the torture & joy of creative puppetmastery
content:
a story of a boredom, procrastination, and creative epiphany

sharing space camp
 

this week I completed and shared my 30 second animation — creative courage in the digital void. today I’ll share the very nonlinear and self-tortuous, winding process of making this animation — the majority of which happened in a single day. this animation is absolutely almost nothing like what I expected — this was part of the gift of this process.

a creative warm up to teaching a course

I started working on this animation a few days after returning from travels — I was feeling groggy and very much brain-offline, to say the least, but felt pressured to talk about and share my new course, sharing space camp — a concept which was, even then, very fuzzy in my head.

a meta-note: for me, making creative work about an offering IS how I find clarity, “launch,” and do “marketing” for the offering itself. whether or not something is paid doesn’t really make a difference for me. for me, creative work is the orbital field around the portal that is the paid offering. thus, it’s in creating and thinking through the creative work — that I process, plan, and prepare for the new offering. this past spring, I made a zine called deconstructing the productivity machine — for my course, creative systems. this time, I felt a general, strong urge to do animation.


listening to the voice in my head

this animation started with a voice in my head — a voice which said,

“the thing is, you are already in outer space. it’s just more comforting to believe that you need to be acknowledged in order to exist.”


I followed that line, and finished writing the text, which you can read in full here. it’s a poetic and philosophical manifesto-y declaration of why sharing your work into the void can be far more empowering than being on social media. I wrote it in an hour or so.

then, I started out by sketching out the thumbnail sketches of each visual — corresponding with each line.

 
 

then, two weeks of boredom & procrastination

after that, I got a little bit… shall we say, bored? I spent the next 2 weeks attempting to sketch out each image in more visual detail, but somehow it felt too constrictive to attempt to “translate” text into visuals.

I learned that in this context, a text-first visual process kills the spontaneity and creative energy of a story. the images felt too “literal” and uninspired. language felt too blunt, crude, and boring for the kind of mysterious, numinous visual experience I wanted to create.

and, I was already feeling a bit overwhelmed, chaotic, and unfocused from re-adjusting to Istanbul life. I wanted the animation to be done yesterday. I felt pressured by this new course I had already committed to teaching, for which students had already signed up. the conflict of these tensions and pressures only made me drag my feet even more…

it took all the self-discipline I had to force myself to sit on the couch on hot summer evenings and sketch for 1-2 hours, absentmindedly, feeling not very connected or passionate or excited, but in more of a monotonous, lazy flow. I went through the motions and did the work.

(1) I developed the still images I had sketched previously.
(2) I made the images move with minimal (3-4) frames each
(3) I tried to think about the cohesive whole, but I realized that the visuals were straying further and further away from the original text.

my course launch date was approaching, and I had spent 2 weeks fiddling around on a half finished animation I was already bored of.

I wasn’t sure what to do.

 
 

“kill it or finish it now” — a one day creative sprint

then, with the familiar feeling of deep creative constipation and agony, I said damn it, I need to finish this in as little time as possible, or kill it entirely — and I’ve already spent too much time on this. let me just do the bare minimum and call it a day.

so, on tuesday night, I imported all my animated images into Adobe Rush. then I woke up on wednesday morning, and put myself on creative sprint mode — which is a sort of hyperfocus intensity where I enter a time warp tunnel and can think of nothing else except this one thing.

I made some crucial decisions —

  • abandon the text entirely, let the visuals tell the story

  • choose music instead of voice over

  • let the film be be way shorter than I expected

  • finish it today — no matter what

I spent the first few hours rearranging and redoing 1/3 of all the visuals — to create a clearer emotional arc, and smoother narrative transitions between images. a lot of it was intentionally thinking about color and symbolism, but much of it was following my intuition and creative flow.

this part felt absolutely magical. it was, as if, once freed from a “script,” I could let the script reveal itself to me.

 
 

enthralled by the possibility of music

after many iterations over several hours, I stitched everything together, and searched for music — a process which felt daunting to me, because I had never done it before.

many years ago, I kept getting ads for Epidemic Sound — and I guess their ad investment paid off, because I got lost in their library. each song felt like a portal, evoking a world of flashing images in me. I limited myself to 1 hour to choose a song that felt resonant — hope and a future, by edgar hopp. then, I spent an hour finding the right clip and editing it until I felt like I was just being obsessive and perfectionist. I forced myself to stop.

I finished the animation around 6 PM, exported it, made K watch it with me like 10 times. I felt very proud of myself.

 
 

what I learned / what’s lingering

the main takeaway I have from this experience is remembering, viscerally, that animation makes me feel so alive — like nothing else, except maybe dance. I felt a high afterwards that made me want to throw myself into life. the last time I felt this high was making an animated poem about sleep in 30 hours over 3 days, in 2021.

as much as I love writing, its beauty happens outside of lived time — it is a slow slow simmering of language, an unfolding that happens over hours, days, or weeks. but the combination of movement, sound, and visual storytelling is visceral and immediate. and yes, it’s often tedious and boring and a pain in the ass to execute — but as a result, it’s also wondrously satsifying to see it come to life.

I felt like a puppetmaster whose wooden puppets had suddenly come alive in the night, and were dancing for me.

the second insight, of course, is that if there will be visuals in a piece of work, visual creation always comes before text. seeing comes before words, wrote John Berger in ways of seeing.

I knew this. I never write something here, on this journal, without first creating the visual image for it. the visual image is never the accompaniment; it is the seed. I never create a course without visuals first.

words put me in the world of defined meanings and abstract concepts, but visuals put me in the realm of subtle, emotional realities and infinitely expanding imagination. words stimulate the flowing of imagination, but visuals create a world with economy and immediate precision.

but, they are both my puppets. I’m eagerly plotting ways to make them dance for me, again.
